The assertion that ACL 2023 material mitigates contamination is unconvincing for models released in 2024–2025, since the papers, abstracts, and videos were already public. No contamination audit or no-context baseline is included; this is especially concerning for generic questions about titles and affiliations.

Prompt-robustness conclusions are based on one random prompt assignment per instance, without repeated draws, per-prompt variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Some alternative prompts also change modality wording, and Section 5.2 conflicts with Figure 2 over whether MCIFfix or MCIFmix was used.

Reproducibility and baseline calibration need improvement: preprocessing and video-frame sampling are underdescribed, model-card default decoding is not fully specified, code is deferred until acceptance, Table 8 contains an incorrect Qwen2.5-Omni checkpoint link, and human/oracle and specialized ASR/MT baselines are absent. Given these central evaluation limitations, the otherwise valuable benchmark falls slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored intersection of crosslingual instruction following, multiple input modalities, and long-form scientific content.

MCIF contains valuable human effort: professionally revised transcripts and translations, expert-authored question-answer pairs, modality-source labels, and largely parallel data that could support controlled analyses.
The empirical study is broad, covering 23 text, speech, video, and multimodal models across four task families, two context lengths, four output languages, and fixed versus varied prompts.
The manuscript is generally well organized, provides per-language results and annotation guidelines in the appendix, and discusses licensing, compensation, and intended resource release.
weaknesses: The scope is substantially overstated. For most tasks, the benchmark contains only 21 talks, about two hours of content and 220 QA pairs, from one narrow domain. Moreover, all source speech and video are English; German, Italian, and Chinese occur only in prompts and textual outputs. Thus this is not fully multilingual across modalities or “parallel across all dimensions” as claimed.

The central claims about audio-visual integration are not supported by the task design. Questions labeled AV are explicitly answerable from either audio or video alone, so no questions require combining complementary evidence from both modalities. Recognition and translation are also fundamentally audio-derived. Consequently, speech-plus-video comparisons do not establish genuine multimodal fusion ability.

QA and summarization rely exclusively on BERTScore, without specifying the encoder/configuration, validating it for all four languages, or supplementing it with human, factuality, exact-match, or LLM-based evaluation. Averaging potentially language-specific BERTScores is questionable. Summarization additionally uses a single paper abstract—not a talk-specific summary—as reference, and negative rescaled BERTScore does not straightforwardly mean “worse than random” as repeatedly asserted.

The prompt-robustness experiment uses only one random paraphrase per example, with no repeated prompt assignments, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests. Several prompts are not semantically equivalent: one German prompt requests a summary “in English,” some prompts refer specifically to audio despite being used across modalities, “verbatim” recognition conflicts with cleaned references, and the fixed German translation prompt is ungrammatical. These artifacts can directly produce the reported wrong-language and robustness failures.

Important analyses are internally inconsistent or selectively constructed. Section 5.2 says MCIFfix is used to avoid bias from MCIFfix's single fixed prompt, whereas Figure 2 reports MCIFmix. Section 5.3 calls Ola the best MLLM although Table 2 shows Gemini 2.5 Flash is substantially better; excluding Gemini changes the conclusion that MLLMs underperform unimodal systems. Cross-family comparisons between different architectures also cannot establish causal effects of modality.

Reproducibility is incomplete: video frame sampling, audio/video preprocessing, truncation, decoding parameters, random seeds, and exact commercial-model version/date are absent. Gemini is missing from the model-details table, and the listed Qwen2.5-Omni checkpoint URL incorrectly points to Phi-4 Multimodal. Default model-specific generation settings further undermine controlled comparison.

There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, annotator-agreement measurements, or independent annotation-quality estimates despite the small test set and often small score differences. The short-versus-long QA construction is insufficiently specified and may confound context length with answer localization or sample selection.

The contamination rationale is unconvincing: public ACL 2023 papers, abstracts, metadata, and presentations predate most evaluated 2024–2025 models, yet no contamination test is performed. Memorization is especially plausible for paper titles, affiliations, and the exact abstracts used as summarization references. Overall, the resource has promise, but the current evaluation does not reliably substantiate several headline claims.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and insufficiently studied intersection: multimodal, crosslingual instruction following over speech, video, and text, including longer inputs and multiple task families.

The aligned benchmark design is useful for controlled modality comparisons. Professional transcription and translation, expert-authored QA pairs, modality-dependence labels, and deliberately unanswerable questions are valuable design choices.

The empirical coverage is broad, with 23 LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and MLLMs; per-language results; fixed and varied prompts; and modality ablations. The observed failures in long-context processing and audio-video integration are informative.

The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and unusually transparent about annotation procedures, compensation, licensing, prompts, model versions, and planned release of data, code, and model outputs.
weaknesses: The benchmark is small and narrow for its broad claims: most tasks use only 21 ACL 2023 talks and 220 QA pairs, while the 100-talk extension applies only to summarization. All source speech and video are English, and the additional languages occur primarily in prompts and outputs. Thus, claims of being multilingual and fully parallel across languages, modalities, and context types are overstated.

The central QA and summarization evaluations rely solely on BERTScore, without human evaluation or complementary measures of factual correctness, answerability, hallucination, instruction compliance, or summary coverage. The exact multilingual BERTScore configuration is not reported. Paper abstracts are also imperfect references for summaries of talks and may contain information absent from the presentation.

The prompt-robustness evidence is weak: MCIFmix appears to sample only one paraphrase per instance, rather than evaluating every instance under all prompts or repeated samples, and no variance or significance analysis is provided. Section 5.2 says MCIFfix is used while Figure 2 reports MCIFmix, creating a consequential ambiguity.

The short-versus-long comparison is confounded by different inference procedures: short outputs are generated segment-wise and concatenated, whereas long inputs are handled in one pass. Short text inputs are not evaluated, and short-form summarization is absent, so context-length comparisons are not fully parallel.

Reproducibility and comparison details are incomplete, particularly model-specific audio/video preprocessing, frame sampling, API snapshot information, and random seeds. Using each model's default generation settings may also confound model quality with decoding choices. Table 8 omits Gemini and incorrectly links Qwen2.5-Omni to Phi-4-Multimodal weights.

Some analyses are selectively or inconsistently presented: Figure 3 describes Ola as the best MLLM despite Gemini obtaining substantially higher long-form QA scores, without explaining the exclusion. No confidence intervals or statistical tests are reported despite the limited number of talks.

The contamination argument is unconvincing. ACL 2023 papers, abstracts, and talks predate several evaluated models and could have appeared in their training data; merely choosing the latest available conference does not establish a clean test set, and no contamination audit is performed.

Annotation quality assurance is underreported: there is no inter-annotator agreement, independent QA verification protocol, or quantitative audit of transcription and translation quality. These omissions matter given the benchmark's modest size and reliance on single-reference automatic metrics.

strengths: Targets an important intersection of multimodal, crosslingual, and longer-context evaluation that is insufficiently covered by existing benchmarks.
The parallel organization across modalities, languages, tasks, and context lengths could support useful controlled analyses.

Data creation represents substantial effort, including professionally corrected transcripts, professional translations, and expert-authored QA pairs with audio-only, video-only, audiovisual, and unanswerable labels.
The evaluation covers a broad set of 23 text, speech, video, and multimodal systems, with per-language results and both open-weight and commercial models.
Annotation compensation, licensing, consent, prompts, and model versions receive more documentation than is typical.
weaknesses: The benchmark is too small and narrow for its broad claims: most tasks use only 21 ACL 2023 talks, two hours of core content, and 220 QA pairs; the 100-talk extension applies primarily to summarization. The purported long inputs are only roughly 5–7 minutes.

Its multilingual and crosslingual scope is overstated. Every source is English, while German, Italian, and Chinese appear principally as translated prompts and targets. This evaluates English-to-X transfer rather than general crosslingual multimodal understanding.

Data contamination is a serious unresolved threat. The public ACL 2023 papers, abstracts, metadata, and videos predate many evaluated 2024–2025 models. Selecting the newest available public material does not prevent training exposure, and no contamination audit is performed.

The central QA and summarization conclusions rely solely on multilingual BERTScore. There is no human validation, factuality assessment, metric correlation study, or dedicated evaluation of correct abstention. Moreover, paper abstracts are imperfect references for talk summaries, so valid outputs may be penalized.

The prompt-robustness experiment is not statistically valid: MCIFmix samples only one prompt per example, without repeated prompt trials, uncertainty estimates, or a reported sampling seed. Some prompts are not equivalent—the German pool includes an instruction to summarize in English, and several prompts mention audio even when applied to other modalities—so measured differences cannot be attributed cleanly to paraphrase sensitivity.

No confidence intervals, significance tests, or bootstrap analysis over talks are provided. Given only 21 core source items and four translated versions of the same underlying content, many small model and modality differences do not support the paper's strong comparative claims.

Annotation quality control is underspecified. The paper does not report independent double annotation, inter-annotator agreement, adjudication rates, or quantitative audits of QA modality labels and translations despite describing the data as verified and expert-vetted.

Important baselines are absent, particularly modular ASR-plus-LLM, ASR-plus-MT, and transcript/OCR-based video pipelines. These are needed to determine whether failures arise from perception, crosslingual generation, reasoning, or multimodal integration.

Reproducibility has concrete errors and omissions: Section 5.2 alternately identifies the modality analysis as MCIFfix and MCIFmix; Gemini is missing from the model-details table; the Qwen2.5-Omni row links to Phi-4-Multimodal; Gemini's exact configuration is unspecified; and video sampling, audio handling, decoding seeds, and BERTScore configuration are not adequately documented.

The QA breakdown claims to use the best model from each family but selects Ola instead of the substantially stronger Gemini 2.5 Flash without explaining an open-model restriction. Combined with model-specific default decoding and system prompts, this weakens the fairness of the comparison.

The work largely repackages four conventional tasks—recognition, translation, QA, and summarization—under paraphrased instructions. It does not evaluate richer compositional constraints typical of instruction-following benchmarks, limiting the novelty of the claimed instruction-following contribution.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and important gap: joint evaluation of instruction following across text, speech, video, languages, and context lengths. The aligned design is distinctive and enables unusually controlled cross-modal comparisons.

The annotation pipeline is substantially stronger than that of many synthetic benchmarks: professional transcription and translation, expert-authored QA pairs, timestamps, modality-source labels, unanswerable questions, and documented licensing and compensation.

The experimental breadth is impressive, covering 23 LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and MLLMs. Per-language results, fixed versus varied prompts, modality ablations, and qualitative failure analysis provide useful baseline evidence.
The benchmark produces interesting findings about long-context degradation, prompt sensitivity, and the limited benefit—and occasional harm—of adding video to speech.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with detailed task definitions, prompts, model versions, annotation guidelines, ethics discussion, and plans to release data, code, and model outputs.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation set is small: most tasks use only 21 talks, roughly two hours of content, and 220 QA pairs. Some reported QA subgroups contain only 17–49 examples. Without confidence intervals, significance tests, or speaker/talk-level uncertainty estimates, fine-grained model comparisons and broad conclusions about model families are fragile.

The claimed multilingual and long-form scope is narrower than suggested. Every source talk is English, so the benchmark evaluates only English-to-target-language transfer rather than diverse source-language speech or video. The talks average about 5 minutes 40 seconds and come from a single conference and domain.

QA and summarization are evaluated solely with BERTScore, without human evaluation or demonstrated correlation on these multilingual scientific outputs. The BERTScore backbone and language-specific configuration are not reported. Moreover, paper abstracts are used as talk-summary references without dataset-specific verification that all reference content occurs in the presentations, creating a potentially unfair source-reference mismatch.

The benchmark does not directly test cross-modal fusion: an AV-labeled question is explicitly answerable from either audio or video alone, rather than requiring complementary evidence from both. Consequently, claims about models' ability to integrate speech and vision are stronger than the task design supports.

Several consequential reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in the analysis. For example, Ola's long-form MCIFmix WER is 6.6 in Table 2 but 36.8 in Table 10; Section 5.2 says it uses MCIFfix while Figure 2 and the surrounding rationale indicate MCIFmix; and the QA breakdown calls Ola the best MLLM despite Gemini 2.5 Flash scoring substantially higher. Table 8 also omits Gemini's configuration and links Qwen2.5-Omni to Phi-4 weights.

The construction of short-form QA inputs is not explained: although answer timestamps and approximately 16-second segments are mentioned, the paper does not specify how questions, relevant segments, and unanswerable cases are paired. This omission makes the short-versus-long comparison difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The prompt-robustness experiment uses only one randomly selected paraphrase per instance, without repeated prompt draws or seeds. Some mixed prompts are themselves inconsistent with the task: a German summarization prompt explicitly requests English output, and several prompts refer to audio even when reused for text or video inputs.

Selecting public ACL 2023 talks does not by itself prevent contamination of 2024–2025 models, especially because the associated papers, titles, and abstracts were publicly available. No contamination audit is provided, despite contamination avoidance being part of the benchmark motivation.

strengths: MCIF addresses a relevant gap by combining text, speech, and video inputs with short- and long-form contexts, four instruction/output languages, and 13 task formulations.
The dataset involves substantial human effort, including professional transcription and translation, expert-authored QA pairs, modality-source labels, and explicitly unanswerable questions.
The empirical study has broad model coverage: 23 LLMs, speech models, video models, and multimodal models, with per-language results and modality analyses.
weaknesses: The headline scope is overstated. The core benchmark contains only 21 English-source talks, roughly two hours of content, and 220 QA pairs from one narrow domain. German, Italian, and Chinese occur primarily as instructions and outputs rather than source speech or video, and the 100-example summarization subset is not parallel to the other tasks.

Evaluation of QA and summarization relies solely on BERTScore, without human evaluation, factuality assessment, alternative metrics, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The BERTScore backbone and language-specific configuration are not documented, making cross-language averages difficult to interpret.

Paper abstracts are used as references for summarizing talks, although abstracts can contain information absent from presentations and omit material emphasized in them. This reference mismatch substantially weakens the summarization scores and the claim that summarization is intrinsically the hardest task.

The prompt-robustness experiment does not evaluate every example under every paraphrase or report repeated trials, seeds, paired statistics, or per-prompt results. Several prompts also change the task: one German prompt requests a summary in English, some prompts refer specifically to audio despite being used across modalities, and Chinese requests 400 characters while other languages request about 200 words.

Important implementation details are missing, including frame sampling, audio/video preprocessing, truncation, model-specific input construction, decoding settings, random seeds, and the exact Gemini API version. The construction of short-form QA examples is also unclear.

There are concrete reproducibility inconsistencies: Section 5.2 alternately identifies the modality experiment as MCIFfix and MCIFmix, the Qwen2.5-Omni entry links to Phi-4-Multimodal weights, and code is simultaneously described as released and as available only after acceptance.

Using public ACL 2023 papers and presentations does not establish freedom from contamination for models released in 2024–2025. No contamination audit or closed-book control is provided, and repeated metadata questions such as author affiliations are particularly vulnerable to parametric recall.

No inter-annotator agreement or independent quality audit is reported for QA answers and modality labels. Combined with the small number of talks and absence of uncertainty estimates, this makes several model-family and modality conclusions fragile.

Comparisons confound input modality with model family, training, size, and input quality—for example, text models receive gold transcripts while speech/video models process raw signals. Consequently, claims that text is inherently easier or that current MLLMs fail to integrate modalities are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: MCIF targets an important gap by jointly evaluating text, speech, video, crosslingual instruction following, and multiple task families in a largely parallel design.

The dataset construction shows substantial effort: professional transcription and translation, expert-written QA pairs, modality-dependence labels, unanswerable questions, and documented annotation guidelines.
The evaluation covers 23 diverse LLMs, SpeechLLMs, VideoLLMs, and MLLMs, with useful modality ablations, language-level results, and qualitative failure analysis.
The fixed-versus-varied prompt setup and release of data, outputs, and evaluation code could make MCIF a useful diagnostic resource.
The manuscript is clearly organized and visually polished, with strong motivation and informative tables and figures.
weaknesses: The scope is narrow relative to the paper's broad claims: the fully featured portion contains only 21 talks and 220 QA pairs, all source content is English, all talks are from one NLP venue, and the target languages are high-resource. Non-English speech or video is never evaluated, and only summarization uses the larger 100-talk set.

Evaluation validity is insufficiently established. Open-ended QA and summarization rely solely on BERTScore, without human evaluation or factuality and answerability metrics; this is especially problematic for short factual answers and unanswerable questions. Paper abstracts are also imperfect references for summaries of talks.

The prompt-robustness experiment uses only one randomly selected paraphrase per instance, reports no repeated draws, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and includes non-equivalent prompts. For example, one German summarization prompt requests an English summary, while several prompts refer specifically to audio even when used for other modalities.

Several inconsistencies weaken confidence in the analyses: Section 5.2 says it uses MCIFfix while Figure 2 reports MCIFmix, and Figure 3 claims to select the best MLLM but uses Ola despite Gemini 2.5 Flash obtaining substantially higher QA scores.

The long-form and contamination claims are overstated. Talks average roughly five minutes and peak near seven minutes, the short-versus-long QA construction is not adequately specified, and using ACL 2023 material does not rule out contamination in models released in 2025, particularly for papers and abstracts.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear, including exact multilingual BERTScore configurations, video frame and audio preprocessing, model-specific context handling, and decoding settings beyond defaults. The model table also gives an incorrect checkpoint link for Qwen2.5-Omni.

Overall, the resource is promising, but its limited coverage and unresolved evaluation issues prevent the central crosslingual, long-context, and robustness conclusions from being sufficiently convincing for acceptance in the present form.
